Per TJC FPPE standards, CPHQ quality review and accountability domain standards, and medical staff privileging principles, proctoring is the standard direct observation mechanism for new privilege competence evaluation.

questions.text: A hospital has implemented a new policy requiring all peer reviewers to complete conflict of interest disclosure forms before participating in any review. The primary purpose of this policy is to

options.a: Reduce the time required to complete peer reviews.
options.b: Protect the legal defensibility and integrity of the peer review process.
options.c: Ensure all reviewers receive adequate compensation.
options.d: Comply with HIPAA requirements for peer review confidentiality.

questions.explanation: Protect the legal defensibility and integrity of the peer review process. Conflict of interest disclosure policies exist to identify and manage potential biases before they compromise the peer review process. When reviewers disclose conflicts and are appropriately recused, the resulting review is more credible, more fair, and more legally defensible — particularly if the review results in an adverse privilege action that may be challenged. Reducing review time (A) is not a purpose of conflict disclosure. Reviewer compensation (C) is an administrative matter unrelated to conflict disclosure. HIPAA (D) governs patient privacy — it is not the regulatory basis for conflict of interest management in peer review. Per HCQIA, TJC peer review governance standards, and CPHQ quality review domain standards, conflict management protects process integrity and legal defensibility.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the reporting of adverse privilege actions to the National Practitioner Data Bank?

options.a: All peer review findings must be reported to the NPDB regardless of outcome.
options.b: Hospitals must report adverse privilege actions that result in restriction, suspension, or revocation for more than 30 days.
options.c: NPDB reporting is voluntary and at the discretion of the medical staff committee.
options.d: Only malpractice payments must be reported to the NPDB — privilege actions are exempt.

questions.explanation: Hospitals must report adverse privilege actions that result in restriction, suspension, or revocation for more than 30 days. Under HCQIA and NPDB regulations, hospitals are required to report to the NPDB any professional review action that adversely affects a practitioner's clinical privileges for a period longer than 30 days — including restriction, suspension, reduction, or revocation. Peer review findings that do not result in a formal adverse privilege action are not reportable (A). NPDB reporting for qualifying adverse actions is mandatory, not voluntary (C). Privilege actions are explicitly reportable — the NPDB covers both malpractice payments and adverse privilege actions (D). Per HCQIA Section 11133, NPDB reporting regulations, and CPHQ quality review and accountability domain standards, the 30-day threshold for adverse privilege actions is the reporting trigger.

questions.text: A quality review committee is designing a new case screening tool. Which of the following criteria is most appropriate to include as an automatic trigger for peer review?

options.a: All cases where the patient expressed dissatisfaction with the hospital food.
options.b: All cases involving an unplanned return to the operating room within 72 hours.
options.c: All cases where the patient was discharged within 24 hours of admission.
options.d: All cases where the patient requested a specific physician.

questions.explanation: All cases involving an unplanned return to the operating room within 72 hours. An unplanned return to the operating room within 72 hours of surgery is a recognized quality indicator signaling a potential complication, technical failure, or clinical management issue requiring review. It is a standard criteria-based screening trigger used in surgical quality programs. Patient dissatisfaction with food (A) is a hospitality complaint, not a clinical quality trigger. Discharge within 24 hours (C) may be appropriate for the diagnosis and is not inherently a quality concern triggering peer review. A patient's request for a specific physician (D) is a patient preference, not a quality trigger. Per AHRQ surgical quality indicators, TJC peer review standards, and CPHQ quality review and accountability domain standards, unplanned return to the OR is a validated, evidence-based peer review trigger.

questions.text: Which of the following describes the concept of "just culture" as it applies to quality review?

options.a: A system that holds all individuals equally accountable for every adverse event regardless of circumstances.
options.b: A system that distinguishes between human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior in determining appropriate responses.
options.c: A system that eliminates individual accountability entirely in favor of system-level blame.
options.d: A system that requires immediate termination for any practitioner involved in an adverse event.

questions.explanation: A system that distinguishes between human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior in determining appropriate responses. Just Culture is a framework developed for patient safety and quality review that recognizes different categories of behavior warrant different organizational responses. Human error (unintentional mistakes) warrants system redesign — not punishment. At-risk behavior (drift from safe practice without awareness of risk) warrants coaching and process improvement. Reckless behavior (conscious disregard for known risk) warrants individual accountability measures. Just Culture does not eliminate individual accountability (C) — it calibrates it appropriately. It does not treat all individuals equally regardless of circumstances (A). It does not mandate termination for adverse event involvement (D). Per AHRQ Just Culture principles, IHI patient safety frameworks, and CPHQ quality review and accountability domain standards, behavioral categorization with proportionate response is the defining feature of Just Culture.

questions.text: A hospital's quality committee is reviewing its utilization of the NPDB. Under federal law, which of the following represents a mandatory query of the NPDB?

options.a: When a practitioner applies for medical staff membership and at least every two years at reappointment.
options.b: When a practitioner submits a complaint against a colleague.
options.c: When a patient files a complaint with the hospital quality department.
options.d: When a practitioner requests a change in their work schedule.

questions.explanation: When a practitioner applies for medical staff membership and at least every two years at reappointment. Under HCQIA and NPDB regulations, hospitals are mandated to query the NPDB when a practitioner applies for medical staff membership (initial credentialing) and at least every two years at the time of reappointment. This mandatory query ensures that any adverse actions reported to the NPDB since the last query — malpractice payments, adverse privilege actions at other facilities — are known to the credentialing organization before reappointment decisions are made. Colleague complaints (B), patient complaints (C), and schedule changes (D) do not trigger mandatory NPDB queries. Per HCQIA Section 11135, NPDB regulations, and CPHQ quality review and accountability domain standards, initial credentialing and biennial reappointment are the mandatory query events.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes delineation of clinical privileges?

options.a: The process of verifying a practitioner's educational and training credentials.
options.b: The specific list of clinical procedures and activities a practitioner is authorized to perform at a given institution.
options.c: The performance data used to evaluate a practitioner's ongoing competence.
options.d: The committee responsible for making credentialing recommendations.

questions.explanation: The specific list of clinical procedures and activities a practitioner is authorized to perform at a given institution. Privilege delineation is the documentation that specifies, in granular detail, exactly which clinical procedures, treatments, and care activities a practitioner is authorized to perform at that specific institution. It is institution-specific — a surgeon credentialed to perform a procedure at one hospital must be separately privileged at each institution where they practice. Credential verification (A) is the credentialing function, not privilege delineation. Performance data (C) informs privilege decisions but is not the delineation itself. The credentialing committee (D) is a governance body. Per TJC Medical Staff Standards, CPHQ quality review and accountability domain standards, and medical staff governance principles, the authorized procedure/activity list is the definition of privilege delineation.

questions.text: A quality professional is reviewing the effectiveness of the hospital's FPPE program. Which of the following indicators would suggest that the FPPE program is functioning as intended?

options.a: The number of FPPE cases initiated has decreased every year for five years.
options.b: All FPPE cases are resolved within the defined evaluation period with documented findings and follow-up actions.
options.c: No practitioners have ever been placed on FPPE in the past three years.
options.d: All FPPE findings are shared publicly on the hospital website.

questions.explanation: All FPPE cases are resolved within the defined evaluation period with documented findings and follow-up actions. An effective FPPE program is characterized by timely resolution of evaluations within the defined period, thorough documentation of findings, and clear follow-up actions — whether that is return to OPPE, continued FPPE, privilege modification, or referral for further review. A decreasing number of FPPE cases (A) may reflect fewer concerns but could also reflect under-utilization of the program — by itself it is not a positive effectiveness indicator. No FPPE cases in three years (C) likely indicates the program is not being used appropriately — in any active medical staff, FPPE should be triggered regularly. Public disclosure of FPPE findings (D) violates peer review confidentiality protections. Per TJC FPPE standards, CPHQ quality review domain requirements, and medical staff governance principles, timely resolution with documented findings and follow-up is the hallmark of effective FPPE program function.
